source_caption:
Ouija: Origin of Evil is one of those rare horror prequels that ends up being stronger than the film it came from. Directed by Mike Flanagan, the story follows a widowed mother and her two daughters who run a fake séance business in 1960s Los Angeles. When they introduce a Ouija board into their act, they unknowingly invite something far more dangerous into their home.

What makes the film work so well is that it focuses on characters before scares. The family feels genuine, making the supernatural events far more unsettling as the story progresses. The relationship between the sisters, especially young Doris and her older sister Lina, gives the film an emotional core that many horror movies lack.

Flanagan also embraces the style of classic horror cinema, using slow-building tension, practical effects, and vintage visual touches that make the movie feel like it could have been made in the 1960s. Instead of relying on constant jump scares, the film creates a creeping sense of dread that grows stronger with every scene.

At its heart, Ouija: Origin of Evil is less about ghosts and more about grief, loneliness, and the consequences of opening doors that should have remained closed. It’s a surprisingly emotional horror film that proves atmosphere and strong characters can be far scarier than loud scares alone.

source_details.synopsis: Ouija: Origin of Evil is a 2016 American supernatural horror film directed, and edited by Mike Flanagan, who co-wrote the script with Jeff Howard. The film is a prequel to the 2014 film Ouija, and stars Elizabeth Reaser, Lulu Wilson, Annalise Basso, and Henry Thomas. It follows a widow and her family who introduce a Ouija board into their phony seance business, thereby inviting a spirit that possesses the youngest daughter. Ouija: Origin of Evil was released in the United States on October 21, 2016, by Universal Pictures.
